cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.prompt: An infant caregiver places a 3-month-old on her tummy on a blanket for short periods several times a day while she is awake and watched. What is the main purpose of this tummy time?

options.a: To help the baby fall asleep faster after her feedings
options.b: To build neck, shoulder, and arm strength for rolling
options.c: To help the baby learn to sit up by herself this month
options.d: To teach the baby to calm herself without being held

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.explanation: Supervised tummy time while awake builds head control and neck, shoulder, and arm strength. Those muscles let a baby push up, then roll over (often around 4 to 6 months), and later sit and crawl. Babies sleep on their backs, so awake tummy time is where this practice happens.

distractorExplanations.a: Tummy time is for awake, supervised play; infants should be placed on their backs to sleep, not on their tummies.
distractorExplanations.c: Most babies sit without support closer to 6 months; a 3-month-old is building head and upper-body control first.
distractorExplanations.d: Self-soothing is an emotional skill; tummy time targets the large muscles needed for rolling and crawling.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.prompt: A toddler teacher is planning indoor movement time for children who are 18 to 24 months old. Which activity best fits their gross motor development?

options.a: Hopping on one foot from one side of the rug to the other
options.b: Riding a two-wheel bike with training wheels in the hall
options.c: Playing a relay race with two teams and a finish line
options.d: Pushing and pulling wagons and climbing low, soft steps

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.explanation: Toddlers from 18 to 24 months are steadying their walking, starting to run, and climbing onto low surfaces. Push-and-pull toys and low, padded steps let them practice balance and leg strength at their own pace, which matches what most children this age can do.

distractorExplanations.a: Hopping on one foot is a skill most children reach around age 4, not in the second year of life.
distractorExplanations.b: Pedaling and steering a bike come years later; even tricycles usually appear around age 3.
distractorExplanations.c: Relay races depend on team rules and waiting turns, which are beyond most children under 2.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.prompt: A preschool teacher is planning outdoor time for a group of 3- and 4-year-olds. Which large-muscle activity fits most children in this age group?

options.a: Pedaling tricycles along a path with gentle curves
options.b: Jumping rope while two friends turn the long rope
options.c: Tracing letters in sand trays at the outdoor table
options.d: Playing a team game of kickball with outs and innings

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.explanation: Most 3- and 4-year-olds can pedal and steer a tricycle, run, climb, and kick a ball. Riding on a path with gentle curves works the legs, balance, and coordination at a level they can succeed at, which is the goal of large-muscle play at this age.

distractorExplanations.b: Jumping into a turning rope takes timing that most children develop around ages 6 to 7, not at 3 or 4.
distractorExplanations.c: Tracing letters builds fine motor and early writing skills; it does not exercise the large muscles.
distractorExplanations.d: Kickball with outs and innings relies on game rules and team strategy that suit school-age children.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.prompt: A family child care provider is setting fine motor goals for the 5-year-olds in her group. Which skill are most children this age learning to do?

options.a: Pick up small cereal pieces with a thumb and finger
options.b: Write full sentences in neat cursive handwriting
options.c: Cut on a line and print some letters of their name
options.d: Scribble on big paper while gripping with a fist

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.explanation: Around age 5, most children are learning to cut along a line with scissors, copy simple shapes such as a triangle, and print some letters, often starting with their own name. Goals should target this emerging skill level so children practice with success.

distractorExplanations.a: The pincer grasp for small objects develops near the first birthday, so 5-year-olds have usually mastered it.
distractorExplanations.b: Writing full sentences in cursive is a school-age skill, well beyond what most 5-year-olds are expected to do.
distractorExplanations.d: Fist-grip scribbling is typical of young toddlers; most 5-year-olds use a finger grip and draw shapes.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.prompt: A director suggests that 4-year-olds complete tracing worksheets each morning to get their hands ready for writing. Which plan gives children more effective fine motor practice?

options.a: Longer worksheet sessions with dotted lines that fade out
options.b: Play dough, tongs, puzzles, and stringing beads
options.c: A daily video that models the correct pencil grip to copy
options.d: Copying letters from the board while seated at tables

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.explanation: Squeezing play dough, picking up items with tongs, fitting puzzle pieces, and stringing beads build hand strength, finger control, and eye-hand coordination through play. These hands-on materials prepare children for writing better than paper drills, and children stay engaged longer.

distractorExplanations.a: More worksheet time adds seated drill but little hand strengthening, and many 4-year-olds lose interest fast.
distractorExplanations.c: Watching a video is passive; children need to use their own hands and fingers to build fine motor control.
distractorExplanations.d: Copying from a board is a teacher-directed writing drill that expects skills many 4-year-olds do not have yet.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.prompt: Mateo, age 4, tells his teacher that his block tower keeps falling down. She wants to help him solve the problem on his own. What is the best thing for her to say?

options.a: "Let me show you how to build it so it stays up."
options.b: "Great job trying! Your tower is really tall."
options.c: "Why don't you build a road instead of a tower?"
options.d: "What do you notice about the bottom blocks?"

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.explanation: An open-ended question that points to the cause of the problem invites the child to observe, think, and test a new idea himself. It supports problem solving and persistence while leaving the solution in his hands, which builds both thinking skills and confidence.

distractorExplanations.a: Demonstrating the fix solves the problem for Mateo, so he misses the chance to figure it out himself.
distractorExplanations.b: Praise is kind but gives Mateo no clue about why the tower falls or what he could change next time.
distractorExplanations.c: Redirecting to a different structure avoids the problem instead of helping him work through it.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.prompt: A 9-month-old watches her caregiver hide a rattle under a blanket, then pulls the blanket away and grabs the rattle. Which cognitive milestone is she showing?
cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.explanation: Object permanence is the understanding that things still exist when they are out of sight. It usually emerges in the second half of the first year, which is why infants this age search for hidden toys and enjoy games like peekaboo.

distractorExplanations.b: Conservation, knowing an amount stays the same when its shape changes, develops in the early school years.
distractorExplanations.c: Symbolic pretend play, such as using a block as a phone, typically appears in the second year of life.
distractorExplanations.d: One-to-one correspondence is matching one number word or item to each object, a preschool math skill.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.prompt: At snack time, a teacher asks Ava, age 3, to put one cup at each chair around the table. How does this routine most directly support early math learning?

options.a: It teaches her to recognize written numerals
options.b: It shows her how to add and subtract groups
options.c: It gives practice matching one item per place
options.d: It helps her memorize the counting words in order

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.explanation: Placing one cup at each chair is practice in one-to-one correspondence, matching one object to one place or person. This concept is the foundation for meaningful counting, and daily routines give 3-year-olds real, repeated chances to use it.

distractorExplanations.a: No written numerals are involved in setting cups at chairs; numeral recognition is a separate skill.
distractorExplanations.b: Adding and subtracting groups comes later and builds on matching and counting objects first.
distractorExplanations.d: Saying number words in order is rote counting; this task is about pairing objects, not reciting.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.prompt: During water play, several preschoolers argue about whether a pinecone will float. What should the teacher do to build their science thinking?

options.a: Tell them the answer and explain why pinecones float
options.b: Ask them to predict, test it, and talk about results
options.c: Save the question for the planned science lesson later
options.d: Show a short video about objects that sink and float

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.explanation: Early science is inquiry: children ask a question, predict, test with real materials, observe, and talk about what happened. Building on a question the children raised themselves, in the moment, keeps their curiosity high and teaches the steps of scientific thinking.

distractorExplanations.a: Giving the answer ends the inquiry; children learn more by predicting and testing it themselves.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting for a planned lesson misses the teachable moment the children's own question has created.
distractorExplanations.d: A video replaces hands-on testing with watching, so children skip predicting and observing results.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.prompt: A toddler teacher sets out a shallow tub of water with cups, sponges, and funnels. A parent asks why the program lets children "just splash." What is the best explanation?

options.a: It keeps toddlers busy while teachers set up lunch
options.b: It helps toddlers practice staying neat and dry
options.c: It is a reward for children who followed the rules
options.d: It builds cause-and-effect thinking and new words

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.explanation: Sensory play lets infants and toddlers learn through touch, sight, and sound. Pouring, squeezing, and filling teach cause and effect and early measurement, and caregivers add words like full, empty, and wet, so the activity supports thinking and language.

distractorExplanations.a: Sensory play is a planned learning activity that needs active supervision, not a way to occupy children.
distractorExplanations.b: Water play is meant to be messy; the goal is exploration, not keeping clothes clean and dry.
distractorExplanations.c: Sensory experiences are part of the daily curriculum for every child, not a prize for good behavior.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.prompt: A preschool teacher is planning a fall art activity. Which plan best reflects process-focused art for young children?

options.a: Set out paint, real leaves, and paper to explore
options.b: Give each child a precut leaf to glue like the sample
options.c: Have children color a leaf outline inside the lines
options.d: Help each child trace a stencil so the leaves match

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.explanation: Process-focused art values exploring materials, making choices, and expressing ideas over a finished product that looks a certain way. Open-ended materials let each child create something original, which builds creativity, fine motor skill, and confidence.

distractorExplanations.b: Gluing a precut shape to copy a sample is a product craft; every result looks alike and choices are few.
distractorExplanations.c: Coloring inside a printed outline is a coloring exercise that limits each child's own ideas and design.
distractorExplanations.d: Tracing a stencil so leaves match puts the focus on a uniform product rather than the child's creativity.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.prompt: A Head Start teacher plays music and invites children to move the way it sounds: slow and heavy, then fast and light. What does this activity support most?

options.a: Memorizing the words of songs line by line
options.b: Learning to sit still and listen to music
options.d: Copying one dance routine the teacher shows

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.explanation: Creative movement asks children to listen to music and invent their own ways to move. It builds balance and body control, gives children a way to express ideas and feelings, and strengthens listening, so it supports physical, creative, and cognitive growth together.

distractorExplanations.a: The music in this activity guides movement; children are not learning lyrics or singing along.
distractorExplanations.b: Moving freely to the music is the point; sitting still would remove the large-muscle and creative parts.
distractorExplanations.d: Copying a set routine limits creativity; here children decide for themselves how to move to each sound.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.prompt: Lily, age 3, is trying to put on her coat, but one sleeve is inside out and she is getting frustrated. Using scaffolding, what should her caregiver do first?

options.a: Put the coat on for her so the group can go outside
options.b: Offer a hint about the sleeve, then let her finish
options.c: Wait without speaking until she figures it out alone
options.d: Tell her she can try this again when she is older

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.explanation: Scaffolding means giving just enough help for a child to succeed at a task slightly beyond what she can do alone, then pulling back. A small hint keeps Lily doing the work, lowers her frustration, and builds her independence in self-care skills.

distractorExplanations.a: Doing the task for her takes away the practice; scaffolding gives the least help needed, not full help.
distractorExplanations.c: Silent waiting gives no support while she is frustrated; scaffolding offers a bit of help in the moment.
distractorExplanations.d: Putting off the task ignores that she is ready to learn it now with a little support from an adult.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.prompt: A parent visiting a preschool sees children building a "zoo" with unit blocks and toy animals. She asks what they are learning. Which answer best describes the learning?

options.a: Mostly sharing toys, since blocks have little academic value
options.b: Mainly cleanup habits, from sorting blocks onto the shelves
options.c: Not much yet; real learning starts with kindergarten work
options.d: Shapes, measurement, planning, and working with friends

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.explanation: Block play is rich, play-based learning. Children compare sizes and shapes, balance and measure, plan a design, solve problems, and negotiate roles and ideas with peers. A pretend zoo adds language and storytelling, so math, science, and social skills grow together.

distractorExplanations.a: Sharing is one benefit, but blocks also build math and science concepts such as shape, size, and balance.
distractorExplanations.b: Cleanup is a small part; the main learning happens while children design, build, and talk together.
distractorExplanations.c: Play is a primary way young children learn; it builds the foundation for later school skills.

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.prompt: Jamal, age 4, uses a walker and cannot stand at the easel during painting time. What is the best way for the teacher to include him in the activity?

options.a: Tape paper to a low table so he can paint seated
options.b: Let him watch the others and choose paint colors for them
options.c: Paint the picture for him while he says what to make
options.d: Plan a separate quiet activity for him during easel time

cda-childcare-readiness-check-physical-c.explanation: Inclusion means adapting the materials or setting so a child with a disability takes part in the same activity as his peers. Moving the paper to a seated, reachable surface lets Jamal paint for himself, using his own hands and ideas alongside the group.

distractorExplanations.b: Choosing colors for others keeps Jamal on the sidelines instead of letting him paint as his peers do.
distractorExplanations.c: Painting for him removes his own fine motor practice and creative choices from the activity.
distractorExplanations.d: A separate activity excludes him from the group; inclusion adapts the same activity so he can join.
